1:
Two of them notice at once that the psalm is made of other psalms. Keil and Delitzsch call it a psalm-song expanded out of the short hymn before it and drawn in part from an earlier psalm, and describe the manner as mosaic, borrowing from a Latin poet the figure of words fitted together like so many little tesserae; where two earlier psalms were composed chiefly out of one prophet, this one takes its pieces out of the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms alike. Adam Clarke reaches the same conclusion historically: the psalm is intimately connected with the preceding, its close is nearly that of an earlier psalm, and what it says about idols seems taken from that psalm and from a chapter of the prophet, from which he infers that it was written after the captivity and may have been used at the dedication of the second temple.

Who is being summoned is less easily settled. Charles Ellicott holds that the priestly class is addressed, as in the psalm before, and grants that the mention of the courts of the house of our God, with the later summons, may extend it to all who stand in covenant relation — possible, he says, but not proved by the evidence adduced. John Calvin argues the other way and then meets it half-way: the psalmist does not appear to be addressing the Levites exclusively but the people generally, since the reasons given for praising God apply equally to all his children and nothing is said here of the night watching; yet since it was the special duty of the priests to lead and to give out the praise before the people, they are primarily addressed and the people included next in order, which the plural courts confirms, one court belonging to the priests and another to all the people. Matthew Henry takes in both, the priests and Levites who stand in the house and the devout who stand in its courts, and observes that those who are admitted to the privileges of the house have most reason to praise and see most reason. Augustine of Hippo presses the standing itself: they were without and now stand within, and if they were to be servants for ever they ought still to praise, how much more as those who may hereafter gain the privilege of sons.

What exactly is pleasant divides them mildly. John Calvin allows two constructions, that the name of God is sweet or that singing his praises is a sweet and pleasant thing, and prefers the second on the ground that the word properly signifies what is seemly or beautiful, a general sense which answers best. Charles Ellicott agrees that it is the singing of the hallelujah, while noting that others take the name as the subject; he would also render the verb play rather than sing. Matthew Henry makes the work its own wages, since it is a heaven upon earth to be praising God, and the pleasure of it should put our mouths out of taste for the pleasures of sin. Adam Clarke counts the reasons as they come, the goodness first and the pleasantness second. On the choosing of Jacob John Gill refuses both the person and the natural posterity as such and takes it of the whole church, Jews and Gentiles alike, chosen from eternity; Charles Ellicott notes that the term rendered peculiar treasure is a covenant-name for Israel and is used elsewhere of private property; and Matthew Henry draws the consequence that if the seed of Jacob do not praise God for so distinguishing a favour they are the most ungrateful people under the sun. C.H. Spurgeon counts the threefold call and asks whether we are so slow in a sweet employ, adding that grace has made its hearers his personal servants and should make their hearts his court-musicians.
5:
The greatness is asserted rather than argued, and each marks how. Matthew Henry observes that where goodness was the matter of our cheerful praises, greatness is the matter of our awful ones, and that the psalmist is most copious here because we are least forward to consider it; the claim is made with assurance, known not only by observation of the proofs but by experience of the divine greatness working on the soul, and with a holy defiance of all pretenders, since between God and them there is no comparison. John Gill distributes the greatness through the persons of the Godhead and grounds the knowledge of each in a different way, the works of creation for one, the revelation of office and grace for another, and inward experience for the third. Adam Clarke simply numbers it, calling the unlimited power one reason and the superiority to every class of being another, since he is the fountain of existence.

Why God does as he pleases is answered in two opposite directions. Matthew Henry makes the pleasure the ground: he does what he pleases because he pleases, and gives not an account of any of his matters; the power is absolute, so that none can control him or ask what he does, and it is almighty, so that if he will work none shall hinder. Adam Clarke reverses the order, holding that all he has done is right and therefore pleasing in his sight. John Gill approaches it by contrast, since sovereignty of this kind is peculiar to the Lord: the most arbitrary and despotic princes cannot do everything they please, while he can and does, even everything. John Wesley only extends the range, to the visible seas and the invisible depths of both the earth and the waters.

What rises from the ends of the earth is disputed. John Gill reports three older readings, one taking it of the mist that went up out of the earth and watered it, another and the paraphrase taking it of the clouds, so called from their elevation, and a father expounding the clouds mystically of the apostles and prophets, raised from a low and mean estate. Charles Ellicott judges a modern undoubtedly right in referring it to that same mist, which watered the whole face of the ground before the useful trouble of the rain, since the passage it is drawn from plainly refers to the story of the creation and the rain is mentioned as coming afterwards; that a different term stands there does not tell against it, the word here being a general one derived from the verb to ascend. Adam Clarke prefers clouds, on the strength of a traveller’s account of the autumnal rains in the east, where seldom a night passes without much lightning in the north-west quarter, and a squall of wind with clouds of dust is the sure forerunner of the first rain. Of the lightnings Charles Ellicott says they are made to bring rain, which was the eastern notion, conceivable enough even in a colder climate when sheets of rain fall after a flash and a peal, and far more so in the tropics; Keil and Delitzsch warn only that the phrase does not mean he makes lightnings into rain; and Matthew Henry finds in the same clause fire and water thoroughly reconciled by divine omnipotence, coming together without the water quenching the fire or the fire licking up the water. Charles Ellicott compares the treasuries of the wind with the caves of the winds in the Greek and Latin poets.
8:
Two of them spend the passage tracing it to its sources, and so make good the claim that the psalm is assembled from older writings. Charles Ellicott observes that the abrupt change from the miracles of nature to the marvels of history is apparently copied from the psalm that follows, and then identifies the verse on the enduring name as taken from the burning bush narrative and the verse on judging the people as taken from the song of Moses. Keil and Delitzsch do the same at greater length: the account of the conquest recalls a whole series of passages, and the language is Deuteronomic throughout except for one relative particle and an Aramaizing construction of the verb rendered slew. They also correct the sense of one word, since the nations are not many but great, the parallel term being meant not of a powerful number but of powerful might. John Gill takes the other reading, counting the seven nations by name and their kings at thirty-one.

The history is otherwise read typically by one and left alone by the rest. John Gill makes the last plague the one particularly mentioned because it was the plague that made the Egyptians willing to let the people go, and finds in the deliverance through the blood of the passover an emblem of a greater deliverance; he takes the conqueror of the nations as a type, and the two kings named as slain by the hand of a lawgiver who was himself a type of one that destroyed the prince of this world. Yet at the mention of the great nations he steps back from his own expansion and reports that an older Jewish commentator refers the words to the kings of Midian or to those next named, adding that this is best. Adam Clarke declines to comment on the smiting of the firstborn at all, referring the reader to the parallel passages.

What the judging of his people means divides the entry at the end. John Gill takes it first of ruling and governing, protecting and defending, pleading their cause and avenging them of their enemies, and distinguishing them by his care so that others see the difference; but he offers a second construction as well, reading it though the Lord judges his people, that is, chastises them in a fatherly way so that they may not be condemned with the world. Charles Ellicott compresses it into three words, that he sees them righted. John Wesley divides the verse between its halves, the judging being that he will in due time plead their cause and the repenting that he will recall the severe sentence he had passed upon them for their sins. Keil and Delitzsch take the whole clause as the hinge of the psalm, since the God who rules so praiseworthily in the universe and in the history of his people is the same yesterday and to-day and for ever, and it is for the good of his proved church that he ever shows himself the living God, in contrast with the idols that follow.
15:
The passage is borrowed and two of them say so at once. Adam Clarke declines to expound it at all, observing that this verse and those to the end of the section are almost word for word the same as an earlier psalm and referring the reader there; he adds a textual note, that one manuscript restores into this place the two verses which the earlier psalm has and this one omits. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same relation from inside: the passage follows that psalm throughout but with abridgments, and the traces of what has been dropped remain, since the particle used here recalls what was said there of the organ of smell in idols that do not smell, just as the breath denied to them here recalls the smelling denied to them there; the clause, they add, is to be rendered that there is no being of breath at all, not a trace of it, in their mouth. Matthew Henry notes the borrowing too, and marks one difference: in the parallel place the inference drawn from the impotence of idols is that we should trust in the Lord, while here it is that we should bless him.

The absurdity is pressed hardest by the two who write for congregations. Matthew Henry begins from the making: being gods of their own manufacture they could have no power but what their makers gave them, and then what power could their makers receive back from them? They had the shape of animals, he says, yet could not perform the least act even of animal life, so that to give them eyes and ears and mouths and nostrils was such a jest that one wonders how reasonable creatures could be so imposed upon; and he draws the moral both ways, that worshipping senseless objects of sense made the worshippers sensual and senseless, so that worshipping a God who is a Spirit should make us spiritual and wise. C.H. Spurgeon calls it the height of insanity to worship metallic manufactures, and thinks it would be less absurd to worship one’s own hands than to adore what those hands have made; idols are fitter to be played with like dolls by babes than to be adored by grown men, and hands are better used in breaking such things than in making them. He turns it on his own readers as well, since the heathen love their abominable deities better than silver and gold, and it were well if as much could be said of the love some professed believers bear their Lord.

John Gill works from the material upward, noting that the substance is gold and silver, the dust and metals of the earth, what a prophet calls thick clay, and that these are themselves the creatures of the God who says the silver and the gold are his; the knowledge of him and the words of his mouth, he adds, are better than either. At the closing verse he records a division that the others pass over: the words may be read as a statement, that those who make idols are as blind and senseless as the idols, or, with some versions and interpreters, as a wish, that those who make them may become so. Matthew Henry and C.H. Spurgeon both take the plain statement, Henry extending it to those who trust in them as well as those who make them.
19:
The closing summons is counted and grouped differently by each. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the call rounds off the psalm by recurring to its beginning, and that where two earlier psalms have a threefold call this one is fourfold through the introduction of the house of the Levites, while the blessing merely wished in the short psalm before has here become an ascription of praise. C.H. Spurgeon reads the same groups as rings that narrow and widen: the house of Israel comprehends all the chosen seed, the house of Aaron is the smaller but more central ring, the tribe of Levi widens it again, and those who fear the Lord are the choicer spirits who are not his in name only — so that reverence may spread from man to man until the whole lump of humanity is leavened. John Gill distinguishes the two priestly houses by office, the Levites being the inferior ministers who had the charge of things in the temple, and reports a Jewish commentator who confines them to the singers, whose work it was to give thanks morning and evening. Adam Clarke declines to comment here as well, referring the reader once more to the parallel verses of the earlier psalm.

What it means to bless the Lord out of Zion is the last question. Charles Ellicott makes it reciprocal: as God is elsewhere said to bless the covenant people out of Zion, so here they bless him out of Zion, that being the place where the relation between them is best and chiefly realised, a localisation made more emphatic by adding the name of the city to that of the hill. Keil and Delitzsch take it as a commission rather than a location, since Zion, from which God’s own attestation of himself is spread abroad, is also to be the place from which his glorious attestation by the mouth of men is spread abroad — and they add that history has realized this. John Gill reports an older reading that takes the words as the very formula of blessing which the houses just named were to use, or a direction how they should bless, and allows the phrase to point both to the persons who were to bless and to the place; he adds that even doorkeepers in the house of the Lord have reason to bless his name for a place there. Adam Clarke keeps his historical setting to the last word, reading the verse as the praise of those whose temple and city have once more been restored, and with whom God now condescends to dwell.
